newsitem.title: GERMANY: German call money eases after Buba currency swaps.
newsitem.headline: German call money eases after Buba currency swaps.

text.p: German call money rates eased to 3.05/08 percent on Tuesday after the Bundesbank helped ease a liquidity bottleneck by offering currency swaps on Monday.

The Bundesbank has confirmed that it is conducting currency swaps but declined to comment on volume or the reason for the move. Market players said the move was helping to push call money rates lower.

Currency swaps are among several tools occasionally used by the Bundesbank to smooth liquidity conditions. The process involves the central bank buying or selling currencies in the cash market and buying them back several days later.
On Monday call money traded between 3.05/10 percent with rates already down from rates of 4.25/50, reached as the market tackled November's traditionally difficult month-end.
Demand for cash in circulation generally increases during holiday seasons and dealers predicted the Bundesbank may inject extra funds at the weekly repo-tender award on Wednesday.

While the use of currency swaps is slightly unusual, dealers stressed that they did not view the move as signalling any sort of shift in policy at the central bank and that swaps were generally not conducted to impact currency market rates.
Dealers said the swaps' volume was likely quite small, around one to two billion marks. Dealers also said the rate was near 3.05 percent.
After Wednesday's tender award, dealers predict that money market rates will ease back towards 3.00/05 percent.

Banks held 39.3 billion marks at the Bundesbank on Monday compared with 39.9 billion marks. Meanwhile the monthly average was unchanged at 39.6 billion. Lombard borrowings stood at 300 million marks on Monday compared with 800 million marks. The Frankfurt Interbank Overnight Average FIONA= was set at 3.09400 percent on Tuesday after 3.09933.
